============================================================
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
“Do Female Village Council Heads in India Change the Mix of Public Goods?”
============================================================

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Randomized Controlled Trial / Instrument‐Based Causal Design  
•  The 73rd Constitutional Amendment assigns one-third of Gram Panchayats (GPs) to be “reserved for women” by a public lottery in every election cycle.  
•  Because reservation status is orthogonal to pre-treatment village characteristics, comparing reserved and un-reserved GPs yields an Intention-to-Treat (ITT) estimate of the effect of *being randomly forced to elect a woman*.  
•  To estimate the causal effect of *actually having a female head* (Treatment-on-the-Treated / LATE), use a two-stage least squares (2SLS) design with:  
  1st stage: FemaleHead_gp = π₀ + π₁·Reserved_gp + X′γ + ε  
  2nd stage: Y_gp = β₀ + β₁·ŶFemaleHead_gp + X′δ + υ  
This is a textbook randomized encouragement design: reservation is the randomly assigned “encouragement,” female leadership is the endogenous take-up.

Why appropriate?  
•  Random lottery ⇒ exogenous variation, eliminating selection into female leadership.  
•  Data are cross-sectional with rich GP-level outcomes; no need for panel methods, but district fixed effects can tighten precision.  
•  365 GPs (265+100) provide adequate power for village-level regressions and clustered inference.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable(s)  
•  Reserved_gp: Dummy =1 if the GP head post was reserved for women in the most recent election (lottery outcome).  
•  FemaleHead_gp: Dummy =1 if the elected GP head is female.

Control group  
•  Unreserved_gp: GPs whose head seats were open (no gender restriction); almost all of these have male heads.

Timing / Variation  
•  Cross-sectional at the electoral term immediately following the lottery.  
•  The key variation is contemporaneous reservation status; no staggered timing needed.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Random Assignment (Unconfoundedness)  
 Reservation status is independent of potential outcomes.  
 Plausibility: Assignment done by publicly observed lottery within each district; highly credible.

A2. SUTVA / No Spillovers  
 Outcomes in one GP are unaffected by reservation status of other GPs.  
 Potential concern: neighboring GPs may share roads or water sources. Reasonably plausible but must be assessed.

A3. Exclusion (for 2SLS)  
 Reservation affects outcomes only through increasing the probability that the head is female, not through other channels (e.g., signaling to higher-level officials).  
 Plausibility: Reasonable; any direct channel would violate political norms and is unlikely.

A4. First-Stage Relevance  
 Reservation strongly predicts having a female head. Empirically, the first-stage F‐statistic is typically > 200 in prior work.

A5. Stable Composition of GPs  
 No differential dissolution, redistricting, or sample attrition by reservation status. Survey design ensured coverage; plausible.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Spillovers / General-Equilibrium Effects  
•  Mitigation:  (i) Include block-fixed effects; (ii) Drop GPs that share borders and test robustness; (iii) Report spatial HAC standard errors as robustness.

T2. Differential Targeting by Higher-Tier Governments  
•  Mitigation:  Collect data on transfers from district/state governments; control for GP-level government grants; show no difference in grants by reservation status.

T3. Measurement Error & Enumerator Bias  
•  Mitigation:  (i) Use objective engineering audits where available; (ii) Double-entry household survey; (iii) Show balance on enumerator assignment across treated/control.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ===== 0. Packages =====
library(tidyverse)
library(lmtest)       # coeftest
library(sandwich)     # Robust/cluster vcov
library(fixest)       # fast, clusterable regressions

# ===== 1. Load Data =====
gp   <- read_csv("gp_level_data.csv")      # one row per GP
hh   <- read_csv("household_survey.csv")   # household-level (optional)

# ===== 2. Merge / Construct Variables =====
gp <- gp %>% 
  mutate(
    reserved     = if_else(res_status == "Reserved", 1, 0),
    female_head  = if_else(head_gender == "F", 1, 0),
    state        = factor(state_name),
    district     = factor(district_id)
  ) %>%
  # Example outcome: # of drinking water facilities in good condition
  mutate(
    water_good_pc = water_good / population   # per-capita scaling
  )

# ===== 3. Balance Check =====
balance_vars <- c("population","sc_pct","literacy_rate","avg_income")
balance_tbl  <- lapply(balance_vars, function(v){
  t.test(gp[[v]] ~ gp$reserved)$p.value
}) %>% bind_cols(balance_vars, p_val = .)

# ===== 4. Main ITT Regression =====
# Y = drinking water facilities (per capita)
itt_mod <- feols(water_good_pc ~ reserved | district, data = gp,
                 cluster = "district")   # cluster at lottery level

summary(itt_mod)

# ===== 5. 2SLS / LATE =====
late_mod <- feols(water_good_pc ~ 1 | female_head ~ reserved | district,
                  data = gp, cluster = "district")
summary(late_mod)

# ===== 6. Robustness: Include Grants & State FE =====
itt_robust <- feols(water_good_pc ~ reserved + log(total_grants) | district + state,
                    data = gp, cluster = "district")
summary(itt_robust)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Based on theory and qualitative evidence:  
•  Female leaders are predicted to invest relatively more in public goods that directly benefit women’s daily workloads (safe drinking water, all-weather road proximity).  
•  Magnitude: Expect ≈ 10–20 percent increase in the *number* or *quality score* of drinking water facilities; negligible or even negative change in irrigation spending.  
•  Complaint data should show alignment: in female-headed GPs, water/road complaints fall, male-oriented complaints may rise.

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Random assignment integrity ………………… 1  
2. No interference between units (SUTVA) …… 0.7  
3. Accurate measurement of outcomes ………… 0.9  
4. Limited attrition / missing data ……………… 0.9  
5. Exclusion restriction for IV …………………… 0.8  
Average score: 0.86 ⇒ high internal validity.

============================================================
